original_value: Problem definition: In modern retailing, frequent discounts are seemingly at odds with the idea that price variation antagonizes loss-averse consumers and hence, diminishes their demand for products and services. Our research question then is whether (or not) loss aversion rules out price variation—and in particular, cyclic pricing. Academic/practical relevance: Pricing and revenue management subject to behavioral considerations are key research areas in operations management. Our approach contributes to this research by highlighting the importance of incorporating heterogeneity in consumers’ behavioral responses in pricing models. Methodology: We model a monopolist selling a product over time to loss-averse consumers who differ in their sensitivity to gains/losses. Although the market is thus segmented, the firm cannot price discriminate among consumers based on that sensitivity. We then characterize the structural properties of the firm’s optimal pricing policy. Results: We show that charging a long-run constant price may be suboptimal and then derive conditions under which the optimal policy is cyclic. These findings establish that loss aversion does not preclude price variation and thereby, underscore the importance of incorporating consumer heterogeneity into pricing policies. Managerial implications: For operations management scholars, our model highlights the importance of heterogeneity in consumers’ behavioral responses to firms’ policies and shows that structurally different insights are obtained from pricing models if this heterogeneity is appropriately accounted for. This approach offers new avenues in pricing and revenue management research. For managers, our model suggests that they could vary prices, under certain conditions, without worrying that price variation will antagonize consumers. Our model offers insights on what these conditions are, which managers may incorporate in devising the pricing policies.

result.paraphrase: Problem statement: In contemporary retailing, frequent markdowns appear to conflict with the view that price changes upset loss-averse customers and therefore reduce demand for goods and services. The question we address is whether loss aversion rules out price variation, especially cyclical pricing. Academic and practical relevance: Behavioral considerations in pricing and revenue management are major topics in operations management. Our study advances this literature by emphasizing the need to include heterogeneity in consumers’ behavioral reactions in pricing models. Methodology: We analyze a monopolist that sells a product over time to loss-averse consumers who vary in their sensitivity to gains and losses. Although the market is segmented, the firm cannot price discriminate among consumers on the basis of that sensitivity. We then identify the structural properties of the firm’s optimal pricing policy. Results: We show that a constant long-run price may be suboptimal and derive conditions under which the optimal policy becomes cyclical. These results demonstrate that loss aversion does not rule out price variation and, in turn, highlight the importance of accounting for consumer heterogeneity in pricing policies. Managerial implications: For operations management researchers, our model underscores the importance of heterogeneity in consumers’ behavioral responses to firms’ policies and shows that pricing models yield structurally different insights when this heterogeneity is properly incorporated. This approach opens new directions for pricing and revenue management research. For managers, the model suggests that they can vary prices under certain conditions without fearing that price changes will antagonize consumers. It also provides insight into those conditions, which managers may use when designing pricing policies.
